Title: Drift-Free Conservative Dynamics from Quantized Interaction Rules
Text:
Drift-Free Conservative Dynamics from Quantized Interaction Rules
Park Junhu,1, 2, ∗Youngsoo Ha,1 and Myungjoo Kang1, 2, †
1Seoul National University
2iTrix Co., Ltd
Conservation laws are conventionally discretized through floating-point flux evaluation, with in-
variants obtained by cancellation of approximate interface contributions and admissible weak solu-
tions selected by reconstruction and Riemann solvers. Here we introduce an operator-level formula-
tion in which conservative dynamics is realized as an exact discrete interaction rule on a quantized
state space. The update is defined by an antisymmetric integer-transfer operator, which enforces
conservation exactly at the arithmetic level and eliminates round-off drift from the primitive evo-
lution [1]. For scalar laws, monotone order-preserving transfers select admissible shock structures
within the primitive update, rather than through flux reconstruction. Numerical experiments show
that the interaction rule preserves high-frequency transport near the Nyquist limit and maintains
sharply localized discontinuities in Burgers dynamics.
The same construction extends to multi-
dimensional problems and systems of conservation laws through oriented, vector-valued integer
transfers. These results indicate that conservative dynamics admits an exact discrete realization in
which both invariance and entropy selection are encoded at the operator level, rather than arising
from approximate flux cancellation.
INTRODUCTION
Conservation laws play a central role in physical mod-
eling, expressing invariant quantities such as mass, mo-
mentum, and energy through local balance relations. In
standard numerical formulations, these laws are realized
by floating-point evaluation of interface fluxes in finite-
volume or finite-difference frameworks [2–7]. Conserva-
tion follows from pairwise cancellation of flux contribu-
tions, while admissible weak solutions are selected by re-
construction procedures and Riemann solvers.
Structurally, this approach represents conservative dy-
namics through approximate flux evaluation in finite-
precision arithmetic. Consequently, invariants are pre-
served only up to machine precision, and the primitive
update depends on rounding behavior, summation or-
der, and reconstruction choices. Although these effects
are usually small, they create a separation between the
formal conservation law and its discrete realization.
In this work, we take a different viewpoint: conserva-
tive dynamics is realized directly as a discrete interaction
process.
Instead of computing approximate fluxes, we
define the primitive evolution by a local antisymmetric
transfer operator acting on a quantized state space [8, 9].
Conservation is then not imposed by numerical cancella-
tion, but is an exact algebraic invariant of the interaction
rule. The resulting method does not approximate a flux-
based scheme at the primitive level; it replaces the flux
representation itself by an exact antisymmetric transfer
operator on a countable state space.
This work does not introduce a numerical approxima-
tion of a continuum equation, but formulates a primitive
discrete dynamics from which the continuum description
emerges.
This representation has two immediate consequences.
First, conservation is exact at every step and is indepen-
dent of floating-point arithmetic. Second, weak-solution
selection is relocated to the primitive update: entropy-
admissible solutions are determined by the monotone,
order-preserving structure of the transfer operator itself
[10]. In this sense, the role usually attributed to Riemann
solvers is not removed, but absorbed into the operator-
level interaction rule.
We therefore interpret conservative dynamics not as
the result of flux balancing, but as the coarse-grained
description of an underlying discrete interaction rule in
which both conservation and entropy selection are en-
coded in the primitive operator.
The continuum flux
appears only as an emergent representation of this in-
teraction, while the primitive dynamics is governed by
exact integer transfer.

NUMERICAL TESTS
We test whether the integer-transfer formulation pre-
serves high-frequency transport and nonlinear shock
structure without introducing drift or excessive smooth-
ing. All simulations use a uniform grid, with identical
resolution and CFL number across the compared meth-
ods. In the Burgers tests, FQNM and the WENO base-
line use the same grid and time step, so differences in
shock structure arise from the primitive update mecha-
nism.

The Burgers tests use the initial condition u0(x) =
sin(2πx/L), for which the Hopf–Lax solution is con-
structed from the corresponding primitive.
The persistence of fine-scale structure through nonlin-
ear interaction indicates that shock formation and prop-
agation are governed directly by the transfer operator,
without requiring a separate Riemann-solver stage. The
observed discontinuities are selected and maintained by
the monotone integer transfer itself; entropy admissibil-
ity is therefore realized at the level of the primitive up-
date rather than through reconstructed fluxes. Although
the transfer has a first-order upwind form, quantization
yields a sharper and more accurately located shock than
the unquantized upwind update and the WENO baseline.
High-frequency content remains localized without exces-
sive numerical diffusion, consistent with the operator-
level encoding of both conservation and admissibility.
The difference from the sampled Hopf–Lax profile does
not indicate a failure of the quantized transfer formula-
tion.
The Hopf–Lax construction gives the continuum
entropy solution, but its direct sampling on a finite grid
need not satisfy the intermediate-state consistency condi-
tion imposed by the discrete conservative update. Thus
the observed discrepancy reflects finite-resolution com-
patibility with the discrete update, rather than an error
of the method. In this setting, an exact discrete solution
is a grid state that satisfies Eq. (3) pointwise at every
time step. The intermediate-state condition requires the
discrete flux differences to produce a single-valued ad-
missible transition across a shock without violating the
monotone transfer structure.
The Appendix presents a Shu–Osher shock–entropy in-
teraction test to illustrate the same operator-level con-
struction in a nonlinear system.
That example shows
that the integer-transfer formulation can sustain coupled
nonlinear and high-frequency features in system-level dy-
namics, while the present text focuses on the scalar case
to expose the core mechanism.
DISCUSSION
The present formulation replaces flux-based recon-
struction, at the primitive level, with a discrete anti-
symmetric transfer operator. Invariance is enforced al-
gebraically by the update itself and is therefore indepen-
dent of floating-point round-off.
Extensions to multidimensional problems and systems
follow from the same operator-level construction, al-
though they are not developed here in detail. This sug-
gests that conservative dynamics may admit a fundamen-
tally discrete realization in which flux-based representa-
tions are replaced by an exact interaction rule that en-
codes both invariance and entropy selection in its primi-
tive structure.
CONCLUSION
We have introduced an operator-level formulation of
conservative dynamics based on exact integer transfer be-
tween quantized states. The resulting update conserves
exactly in integer arithmetic, avoids round-off drift, and
encodes entropy selection through a monotone order-
preserving transfer rule. Numerical tests show that this
structure preserves high-frequency transport and sharp
nonlinear discontinuities, indicating that flux-based con-
tinuum descriptions can arise as coarse-grained represen-
tations of an exact discrete interaction rule.
Extension to nonlinear systems
The integer-transfer formulation introduced in the
main text extends directly to nonlinear systems of con-
servation laws.
In this setting, the state becomes a
vector-valued integer field, and the interface transfer is
applied componentwise. The antisymmetric structure of
the transfer ensures exact conservation for each compo-
nent, while intercomponent coupling enters through flux
splitting.

FIG. 4. Shu–Osher shock–entropy interaction. The integer-
transfer formulation propagates the shock and fine-scale os-
cillatory structure with minimal artificial dissipation.
The Shu–Osher problem combines a strong shock with
high-frequency entropy waves and is widely used as a
stringent test of numerical dissipation and resolution.
Figure 4 shows that the integer-transfer formulation
propagates both the shock and the oscillatory structure
without significant smoothing at the grid scale. The os-
cillatory features remain clearly resolved after interaction
with the shock.
This behavior indicates that the transfer rule pre-
serves fine-scale structure during nonlinear evolution
while maintaining exact conservation.
This example
is not intended as a comprehensive stability study for
systems, but rather as representative evidence that the
operator-level construction extends naturally beyond the
scalar setting.
